purpose: Reviewed editorial selections; catalogue facts and coordinates are retained separately. This is not a public content schema.
doam: A monumental Mughal mosque whose red sandstone, marble domes and open courtyard frame the western edge of Lahore's royal precinct.
Major Mughal sacred architecture; distinct from the inscribed Fort and Shalamar property.
Glazed tilework, calligraphy and corner minarets make this mosque a vivid encounter with Lahore's Mughal craft traditions.
Decorative arts and living sacred heritage in the historic city.
A garden mausoleum at Shahdara, with arcaded rooms and a central burial chamber finished in Mughal ornamental detail.
Royal funerary architecture beyond Lahore's walled city.
The remains of an Indus city near Sahiwal illuminate early urban life through excavated streets, working areas and substantial brick structures.
A foundational Indus archaeological landscape outside the provincial capital.
Temples, a sacred pool and associated historic buildings form a layered religious landscape in the Salt Range.
Hindu sacred heritage and architectural diversity in Chakwal.
Massive rounded bastions enclose a desert stronghold in Cholistan, expressing the defensive architecture of southern Punjab.
Desert fortification and a geographically distinct southern context.
A tapering brick tower faces a large water tank and island pavilion, bringing Mughal commemoration and landscape engineering together.
Water architecture and Mughal landscape design in Sheikhupura.
An octagonal, tiered mausoleum in Multan combines brick, timber and glazed tilework in a powerful architectural silhouette.
A defining southern Punjabi funerary monument and sacred destination.
The surviving tiled walls and corner turrets of this octagonal tomb reveal the construction and ornament of Uch's funerary architecture.
Uch Sharif's distinctive brick-and-tile tomb tradition.
A hilltop fort above Kot Diji preserves monumental gateways and bastions associated with Sindh's historic defensive landscape.
A major Khairpur fort, separate from prehistoric settlement remains.
Fortified walls follow the rugged terrain of Ranikot, creating an unusually expansive meeting of architecture and landscape.
A substantial fortified enclosure marks the approach to the Thar landscape, with towers and gateways defining its defensive form.
Thar's fort-building tradition and regional gateway.
A fortified complex in Umerkot connects the historic town with the political and architectural history of eastern Sindh.
Carved sandstone tombs near Karachi preserve a distinctive funerary vocabulary of geometric and figurative ornament.
A major regional stone-carving and burial tradition.
Fortifications, streets and a mosque survive at this historic port beside Gharo Creek, tracing a long sequence of settlement and exchange.
Coastal urban archaeology and Indian Ocean connections.
Brick vaults, domes and intricate blue-and-white tilework shape this mosque's courtyards and prayer spaces in Thatta.
A major example of Sindh's tilework and sacred architecture.
Stone halls, carved details and a corbelled dome survive at this Jain temple in Tharparkar's historic sacred landscape.
Jain architectural heritage in the desert region.
A substantial late-1920s residence in Karachi records the city's mercantile architecture and later civic history.
Twentieth-century urban heritage and coastal-city representation.
The shrine of Sindh's poet-saint brings together a mausoleum, mosque and courtyard adorned with local tilework and decorative craft.
Living sacred and literary heritage in Matiari.
Inscriptions cut into three boulders preserve Ashoka's edicts in Kharosthi, linking this landscape to ancient routes and governance.
Epigraphic heritage and the historical routes of Hazara.
A Buddhist stupa and monastic complex near Khanpur preserves a distinctive cruciform plan within a sheltered landscape.
A major Haripur Buddhist site outside Taxila's inscribed component inventory.
A central stupa, smaller votive monuments and associated structures preserve a major Buddhist precinct in the Swat valley.
Excavated Buddhist architecture and Swat's archaeological sequence.
A courtyard mosque in Peshawar's historic city combines minarets, domed prayer spaces and painted floral decoration.
Living Mughal sacred architecture in Peshawar.
A historic enclosure in Peshawar preserves layers of pilgrimage, caravanserai use and religious architecture within the old city.
Layered urban heritage, rather than a single-period monument.
Carved timber, coloured glass and courtyard rooms express the architectural culture of Peshawar's historic merchant community.
Domestic architecture and Central Asian trade connections.
Ashoka's edicts, inscribed on large rock surfaces in Kharosthi, offer a direct encounter with ancient written history.
Major epigraphic monument in the Mardan landscape.
A prominent Peshawar fort records successive rebuilding and changing military power through the city's history.
Defensive architecture complements the regional Buddhist and sacred inventory.
A settlement mound near Quetta has yielded pottery and architectural evidence central to the study of Balochistan's early communities.
A significant excavated sequence in the Quetta valley.
This mound near Quetta preserves an important sequence of early settlement and changing pottery traditions.
Foundational evidence for early village life in Balochistan.
An archaeological settlement on the Kachi plain preserves evidence connecting regional communities with the Indus urban tradition.
A major settlement sequence complementing, not duplicating, Mehrgarh.
This archaeological settlement near Khuzdar offers evidence of the Kulli cultural tradition and its wider regional connections.
Kulli archaeology and southern interior geographic spread.
A settlement mound in northern Balochistan preserves traces of mud-brick buildings and a long history of occupation.
Northern settlement archaeology documented in the institutional catalogue.
A fortified archaeological site beside the Dasht river plain illuminates the western reach of the Indus world.
Western Indus archaeology and the Makran landscape.
A stone-and-timber residence in Ziarat is associated with Muhammad Ali Jinnah's final months and the history of modern Pakistan.
National commemorative heritage and a distinct upland architectural context.
The ancestral graveyard of the Jams of Lasbela combines carved stone graves, canopies and other funerary structures.
Lasbela's regional funerary craft and ruling history.
A group of carved stone tombs in the Lasbela landscape preserves a funerary tradition related to that of southern Sindh.
Cross-regional stone-carving traditions in southern Balochistan.
Timber-framed rooms and carved architectural details shape a historic fort-palace within the Shigar valley.
Mountain fort-palace architecture and historic conservation value.
A stone-and-timber palace with courtyards and gardens preserves the domestic and ceremonial setting of Khaplu's former rulers.
A major Balti palace, distinct from sacred and archaeological sites.
An elevated, timber-and-stone mosque overlooks Khaplu, with verandahs and prayer rooms expressing local mountain building traditions.
A major example of Balti sacred architecture.
A compact timber-framed mosque in Shigar brings together carved beams, stone infill and layered roof forms.
Historic craft and intimate sacred architecture.
Buddhist figures and Tibetan inscriptions carved into a large boulder preserve an important chapter of Skardu's religious history.
A fort complex above Skardu records the valley's strategic history and successive phases of construction.
Defensive heritage and a commanding valley setting.
Carvings and inscriptions on boulders beside the Indus document travel, religious expression and cultural exchange.
Upper Indus epigraphy and long-distance cultural contact.
Rock carvings near Chilas preserve Buddhist narratives alongside other imagery from the long history of the Indus corridor.
A major rock-art landscape with varied cultural traditions.
A historic khanqah in Thagas preserves the architectural and religious traditions of the eastern Baltistan valleys.
Sacred architectural heritage beyond the principal towns.
A historic polo ground near Khaplu's palace records the relationship between public space, recreation and local cultural life.
A cultural landscape broadening the inventory beyond buildings.
Terraced defensive structures beside the Neelum River preserve an important part of Muzaffarabad's historic landscape.
A principal urban fort and historic defensive position.
A stone temple and enclosure above the Neelum valley preserve a major sacred site with distinctive architectural details.
A regionally important sacred and architectural monument.
The surviving remains of a hill fort near Sharda record the valley's strategic routes and nineteenth-century military history.
Defensive history separate from the nearby temple.
A fortified hilltop structure in Sudhnoti preserves gateways, chambers and evidence of regional military architecture.
Geographic representation of Sudhnoti and its fort-building history.
Stone walls and gateways above the Jhelum preserve a fortified position in the Mangla landscape.
River crossings and regional defensive architecture.
A hilltop fort now surrounded by the Mangla reservoir preserves substantial defensive walls and internal structures.
A major fort landscape with a transformed waterside setting.
A multi-level fortified complex near Samahni preserves the architecture of changing regional powers.
A historic caravanserai on the Bhimber route records the infrastructure of travel, lodging and exchange.
Historic route architecture adds a different building type.
Decorated stone pavilions near the river confluence preserve a distinctive architectural layer of Muzaffarabad's history.
Civic and commemorative architecture alongside the fort inventory.
A stone temple with a shikhara and surviving interior niches preserves sacred architectural heritage in the Kotli hills.
Religious diversity and Kotli district representation.
Gateways, cells, a mosque and a mausoleum surround the courtyard of this fortified roadside complex.
Historic travel infrastructure and Gakhar-period associations.
An octagonal tomb associated with the Gakhar rulers preserves a compact funerary structure near the Pharwala landscape.
Gakhar funerary heritage; retain all derived boundary contexts.
Surviving stone gateways and defensive walls mark a historic Gakhar stronghold in the Soan valley landscape.
A major regional fort; current overlapping boundary contexts are retained.
Rock shelters, a spring and surviving built features preserve an archaeological landscape along the Margalla foothills.
Rock-shelter heritage and the capital's older settlement landscape.
The stone base and architectural remains of a Buddhist stupa survive in the Margalla landscape.
A protected Buddhist archaeological site within the capital territory.
A brick temple with a shikhara, arched openings and traces of painted decoration records a historic sacred layer of Golra.
Religious diversity and surviving temple architecture.
Temples and a dharamshala at the foot of the Margalla hills preserve an older architectural layer within today's capital.
Historic settlement and sacred architecture in Saidpur.
A historic stone railway station and its railway collection connect the capital region with the material history of rail travel.
Transport heritage and a collection-based experience.
A marble mausoleum at Golra Sharif commemorates the Sufi scholar Meher Ali Shah and remains part of a living sacred setting.
Twentieth-century sacred architecture and living cultural continuity.
The shrine of Bari Imam is a major sacred place in the capital region, with a history of patronage and continuing devotion.
